book_context: Late in the book, after an omitted chapter of travel and silence, Adams reaches sixty while his closest friends hold power. John Hay is ambassador in London and then Secretary of State; Lodge is a Senator; Roosevelt follows. Clarence King and Hay are declining. The recurring mechanisms carry forward: 'a friend in power is a friend lost'; sitting on the steps of Ara Coeli; Pteraspis, Lyell and Limulus from the Darwinism chapter; women and the Virgin as force; and the search for unity against multiplicity, now recast as attempts to measure history mechanically. These chapters move from diplomatic triumph to the dynamo and the Virgin, then to magnets, geology and Russian inertia. They prepare the formal 'Dynamic Theory' and the 'Law of Acceleration'. Omitted chapters (Chicago, Silence, Grant, Eccentricity) leave some setup that must be glossed locally: Hay sent to London; the dynamos first seen at Chicago in 1893.

essential: Opening: at sixty, in the London of 1898, Adams feels the family's 150-year effort to bring England into an American system fulfilled by chance under Hay. State locally that Hay is the American ambassador in London.
For the first time he senses purpose or law in history. He is cooler toward the Philippines and accepts Porto Rico; keep his West Indies policing argument in brief.
Surrenden in Kent: the Camerons' house, and the July 4 telegram of the Spanish fleet's destruction framed as Elizabeth's Armada. Later Hay is summoned to the State Department.

The friends' decision that a member of the Government cannot refuse service. Adams's view that office is poison of the will. Hay takes office 'at cost of life', which must stay Adams's fear, not a narrated outcome.
Return to Washington; 'another false start'. Mrs. Hay arranges daily afternoon walks and tea to save the personal relation.

1899 with the Lodges: Sicily as anarchy without sequence, and Ara Coeli drawing all journeys to a centre. America's stride to empire makes 1860 seem as remote as Brutus and Cato, a truth Americans dislike to hear, so he sits silent.

Assisi and St. Francis's rejection of the whole problem. Contrast with the 1874 Assistant Professor's mock epitaph claiming to be first to explain Sac and Soc: keep the Latin epitaph or paraphrase its satire, and note the credit belongs to Maine and Sohm. Law proved as futile as politics and religion.
Summer of solitude in Paris: he begins his 'final profession', a methodical triangulation of the twelfth century in small churches.

La Farge's arrival: his indirect, contradiction-tolerant mind against the American straight-line mind. The Whistler dinner shows art versus talk. La Farge's insubordinate glass leads Adams back to Chartres.

Boer War as a personal outrage tied to 1776 and John Adams, which he keeps from Hay. McKinley's 'pooling' of interests; Pauncefote as Hay's only ally; Hay's speech on the obstructive one-third of the Senate and the 'three duties' of a Secretary of State, which can be condensed but keep the rhetorical question at its end.
Hay's gaiety wearing into the routine of office ('To a head of bureau, the result seemed ennobling').

Close: the ambition to correlate the twelfth and twentieth centuries mathematically despite knowing only s = gt^2/2. Langley's doubting temper and his gift of Stallo's book. 'Adams read and failed to understand'. History needs unity and motion. He settles by the Trocadero on May 12.
optional: Detailed description of Surrenden's avenues, deer-park and Anderida.
Catalogue of shrine names (Karnak, Ephesus, Delphi...) can be shortened to two or three.
Comparison of Hay with other American ministers in London (end of p2).
List of New York school figures (Hewitt, Evarts, Whitney, Tilden) and Harrison's 'There is no politics in it'. Cut together with the Hewitt/Cleveland parallel.
Cassini/Holleben/Clan-na-Gael press-interference detail in p23, beyond a one-line mention.
La Farge's travel tableau (kava, cha-no-yu, bo-tree) can be trimmed to one image.
Newcomb and Gibbs mentions in p26; keep Langley.
risks: The Latin epitaph's line layout may not survive; a paraphrase of its satire is acceptable.

title: INDIAN SUMMER (1898-1899)

verbatim.purpose: Ironic family-historical frame for the Anglo-American rapprochement.
verbatim.text: the sudden appearance of Germany as the grizzly terror which, in twenty years effected what Adamses had tried for two hundred in vain--frightened England into America's arms--seemed as melodramatic as any plot of Napoleon the Great.

verbatim.purpose: Key statement linking the lifelong search for law to his failure as a teacher.
verbatim.text: Never before had Adams been able to discern the working of law in history, which was the reason of his failure in teaching it, for chaos cannot be taught
After all, friends had done the work, if not one's self, and he too serves a certain purpose who only stands and cheers.
In his fancy, office was poison; it killed--body and soul--physically and socially.

verbatim.purpose: Characteristic accumulating dashes; defines the poison precisely.
verbatim.text: his poison was that of the will--the distortion of sight--the warping of mind--the degradation of tissue--the coarsening of taste--the narrowing of sympathy to the emotions of a caged rat.
his obedience to the President's order was the gloomiest acquiescence he had ever smiled.

verbatim.purpose: La Farge's standing reproach; a hinge between Bostonian reason and artistic nuance.
Aphorism stating the chapter's tension between politics and education.
verbatim.text: Practical politics consists in ignoring facts, but education and politics are two different and often contradictory things.

voice_profile: Third-person autobiography in which the elderly Adams treats his younger and present self with ironic detachment ('Adams', 'one', 'the student', 'the tourist', 'an insect', 'the monkey'). Long periodic sentences turn on qualification and paradox. Cosmic science metaphors (force, mass, inertia, triangulation, attraction) are applied to politics and friendship. He undercuts himself constantly through self-deprecation and mock-pedantry. He flatly refuses certainty ('knew no more than...'). Aphoristic closers end paragraphs. Foreign tags and verse quotations act as punctuation. Grief appears only obliquely, through restraint and stage-images. Double hyphens mark interruption and accumulation.
